en: The Buddha-spoken Sūtra of Jyotiṣka, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Liu Song Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "There was an elder named Jyotiṣka, whose storehouses were overflowing with gold."
He was fully endowed with silver, and his male and female servants were well-ordered and lacked for nothing.
There was a white cotton hand-towel hanging by the edge of the pond; when a celestial wind arose, it blew the towel before the king’s palace.
The King immediately convened a great assembly of his ministers to deliberate together, arranging divinations and inquiries to investigate the cause of this marvel.
All the ministers said, "The kingdom is about to flourish; Heaven has bestowed upon us these white cotton cloths."
Jyotiṣka remained silent and said nothing.
The king said to Jyotiṣka,
"All the ministers are joyful, yet you remain speechless."
Jyotiṣka replied, "I dare not deceive Your Majesty.
This handkerchief for wiping tears belonged to my household; it was hanging by the edge of the pond when a celestial wind arose and blew it before the king’s palace."
"For this reason, I remained silent and did not speak.
A few days later, flowers of nine colors, as large as chariot wheels, were encountered as a celestial wind arose and blew them before the king's palace.
The king convened a great assembly of his ministers to deliberate together, arranging divinations and inquiries while marveling at the cause of these wonders.
All the ministers said:
"The state is about to flourish; Heaven has bestowed upon us golden flowers."
Jyotiṣka remained silent and said nothing.
The king said to Jyotiṣka,
"All the ministers are joyful, yet you remain speechless."
Ti-ga replied, "I dare not deceive Your Majesty.
These are withered flowers from the rear garden of my household; they encountered a celestial wind that blew them before the King’s palace."
"For this reason, I remained silent and said nothing.
The King said to Jyotiṣka:
"Such is the state of your family!"
The King commanded his ministers to issue strict instructions to his household to prepare extensive provisions, saying, "I must return and lead two hundred thousand followers to your house to visit.
Tiṣya replied, "I pray that Your Majesty will accompany me;

in my house, couches and mats will appear spontaneously without needing to be spread, food and drink will appear spontaneously without needing to be prepared, things will be brought forth spontaneously without the need for calling, and things will be taken away spontaneously without the need to look back."
The king led a host of two hundred thousand and entered directly through the southern gate of Jeta’s Grove.
Within the palace was a young boy, whose countenance was upright and handsome, his complexion full and radiant, and most endearing to behold.
The king said to Jyotiṣka, "Is this the son of your house? He replied:
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty;
he is a slave who guards the gate of my household.
He advanced a short distance further until he reached the inner chamber, where there was a young girl, her features perfectly formed, her complexion full and radiant, and exceedingly lovely.
The king said to Jyotiṣka,
"Does your family have a daughter? He replied:
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty;
she is a maidservant who guards the gatehouse of my household.

He stepped forward a little further until he reached the front of Jyotiṣka’s hall, where the walls were made of white silver and the floor of crystal. Upon seeing this, the king thought it was flowing water and hesitated, unable to proceed.
Jyotiṣka then led the king forward to enter; he had the king step onto a golden bed and sit upon a jade desk.
Jyotiṣka’s wife emerged from within a heavy curtain of gold and silver, one hundred and twenty *zhuǎn* thick, and prostrated herself before the king, tears falling from her eyes.
The king said to Jyotiṣka, "Your wife prostrated herself before me; why did she weep with tears falling from her eyes? He replied:
“I do not dare deceive Your Majesty!
It was because I smelled the smoke from Your Majesty that tears fell from my eyes.
The King said:
"The common people burn fat, the feudal lords burn beeswax, and the Son of Heaven burns lac; yet none of these produce smoke or fumes—how could they cause tears to flow?
Jyotiṣka said, "Your servant does not dare to deceive Your Majesty."

"In my home, there is a divine 'bright moon' pearl hung in the hall; day and night, it requires no light from fire. Your Majesty is the king of all that emits smoke; therefore, you have smelled its fragrance."

In front of Jyotiṣka’s hall stood a twelve-story high tower; he took the king up there to look about, gazing east, west, south, and north, remaining in a state of dark, restless distress for an entire month.
The minister said to the king:
"The affairs of state are of great importance; we must return to attend to the people.
The king replied:
"In a short while, it may become slightly more bearable.

Thus, Jyotiṣka again led the king’s consort into the rear garden to view the flowing springs and bathing pools; each was beautiful and exceedingly lovely, yet she remained in a state of deep distress for another month.
The minister said to the king, "State affairs are of great importance; we must return home to attend to the people.
The king replied:
"Ah! In a brief moment, it will be slightly more bearable.
Thus, Jyotiṣka bestowed his seven treasures, silks, brocades, and embroideries, along with two hundred thousand people, horses, and chariots, and they all returned to the kingdom at once.
The king immediately convened a great assembly of his ministers to sit together in consultation; he set out various means of divination and questioned them about the cause of this marvel, saying:
"Jyotiṣka is my subject, yet his women and dwellings exceed those of mine."
"I wish to attack him; can he be captured?
All the ministers replied, "He should indeed be captured."
The king led a host of four hundred thousand, beating bells and sounding drums, surrounding the house of Jotika for more than several hundred layers.

Within the gate of Jotika’s residence stood a strongman who, with a single brandish of his hand holding a golden mace, caused all four hundred thousand men and horses to fall simultaneously; their limbs twisted and contorted, their waists and hips bent and crooked, appearing like those intoxicated, with heads and feet limping and staggering, unable to rise again.
Jyotiṣka, riding upon a cloud-chariot in the midst of the void, came and asked the people:
"For what purpose have you come? Why do you lie on the ground and not rise?

"The Great King has sent us to attack the elder," they replied. "At the gate stood a powerful man who, with a single brandish of his golden mace, caused four hundred thousand men and horses to fall prostrate. Their waists and loins were twisted and contorted; they appeared as if intoxicated, their heads and feet limping and crippled, unable to rise again."
Jyotiṣka asked the people,
"Would you like to obtain it?
and all the people replied:
“May you arise! Śrīgupta raised a single divine staff, causing four hundred thousand people, along with their horses, to rise and return to the kingdom.
The King immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Śrīgupta.
"I shall go together with you in the carriage to the place where the Buddha resides. He asked,
"World-Honored One!"
“Jyotiṣka was my minister; what meritorious deeds did he perform in a previous life that his wife and residence surpassed mine in excellence?
The Buddha said:
“Jyotiṣka and five hundred caravan leaders, leading their merchants, were carrying precious treasures as they passed through a perilous road.”
At that time, he saw a sick practitioner in the deep mountains; he provided him with a hut and thick bedding,
supplied him with water, broth, needles, and grain,
and gave him lamps and candles.
At that time, he made a vow, praying for the merit of offerings to the heavenly realms;
now he has obtained the karmic fruit thereof. Who was the donor at that time?
Jyotiṣka was that person; the sick man was my own self;
and all five hundred merchants attained the path of Arhatship.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the king and his ministers gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
This concludes the *Jyotiṣka Sūtra*.
